BasePK: 3310477

Speech:
Madam Speaker, today we will be dealing with Bills C-70, C-71 and C-74. Tomorrow we will go on with C-73 and C-72. Those are the bills relating to the estimates and your ruling, Madam Speaker. We have an agreement, as you well know, to have one speaker from each party for all stages with speeches to be limited to 30 minutes. Those five bills should require all the time today and tomorrow.
In so far as Monday is concerned, we will resume debate at the second reading stage of the following bills: C-58, S-6 and C-12.

July 2, 1981
Business of the House
[ Translation]
This evening, there will be a memorial service on Parliament Hill at 7.30 for Terry Fox. Under these circumstances, Madam Speaker, I have consulted my colleagues of both opposition parties and we have agreed that there will not be any private members' hour today and that the House will adjourn at seven o'clock this evening. Therefore, I have a motion which will receive unanimous consent and that I shall read in a few moments. But first, regarding the business of the House for next week, apart from the three bills I have just mentioned, namely Bills C-58, S-6 and C-12, which will be considered on Monday, I have submitted a list of bills to my colleagues and we shall be in a position Monday to choose from this list a series of bills with which we can proceed in the next few days and which can probably go through all stages before we adjourn next week or the following week, depending on the circumstances.

Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre:
That the private members' hour this afternoon be suspended; that the House continue to sit today until 7 p.m. on Government Orders, and that it adjourn at 7 p.m. today until 11 tomorrow morning.

BasePK: 3310541

Speech:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise on a point of order. I would like to ask about two questions, question No. 30 and question No. 136. Question No. 30 has now been on the order paper for five years and 22 days. Over those five years, I have
Order Paper Questions
raised this matter at least six or seven times or more, and every time I have raised it either the present parliamentary secretary or his predecessors has said he would look into the matter and the question would be answered soon. That has gone on now for five years and 22 days, which I think is a pretty ridiculous situation.
The question merely asks for the names of the members of the Canadian Transport Commission who have Air Canada passes or any of its employees who have Air Canada passes, and if any of the wives of members of the Canadian Transport Commission have Air Canada passes. This is a very simple matter, and yet for five years and 22 days the government has failed to answer. This can only lead to the obvious conclusion that there are people who have passes and that they do not want to let the public know about it.
I think that is shameful. Something should be done by this government to get off its behind. Perhaps hon. members opposite should borrow a bunch of hearing aids so that they can hear what is being raised by the opposition in this House by way of points of order and they can do something about them.
Question No. 136 is the other question. It has been on the order paper for about two years. It concerns the fact that the Liberal Party of Canada chartered a DC-8 from Air Canada in the 1979 election campaign and never paid the bill. By the time of the election a year later the bill had still not been paid, yet Air Canada gave the Liberal party another aircraft. I would like to know what is going on.
I am told that eventually the bill was paid. How much was paid? The Liberal party argued it was being overcharged, whereas the Conservative party paid its bills as they were rendered without disputing them. It is obvious there is a charge. If there is an indebtedness, it should be paid. It is taxpayers' money. Hon. members opposite have never answered that, and I do not understand why they want to hide this matter. An official of Air Canada told my office six months ago that the answer to this question was prepared and in the hands of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin).
Why are the answers to question No. 30 and question No. 136 being held back to the extent of five years and 22 days and two years?

BasePK: 3310545

Speech:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a further point of order. Would the parliamentary secretary undertake to contact personally the Minister of Transport who is, I presume, responsible for the production in the House of the answers to both these questions, and to ask him why something has been in his office for six months and not forwarded on to the Privy Council Office? Will the parliamentary secretary ask the minister why for five years and 22 days information requested about the Canadian Transport Commission should be refused?
I think it is the duty of the parliamentary secretary, if things are stalled like this, not to tell the House it is not his problem, other than to produce answers when furnished to him. I think it is his duty to go after those who do not furnish answers and to ask them what is going on. The parliamentary secretary should indicate that he is being asked about certain questions in the House and should say, "Give me the answer." Giving statistics about the fact that the government answered three of my questions today or that it will answer four tomorrow, or other questions coming up, is no answer at all. Facts, figures and percentages are what we have been getting from the parliamentary secretary and the Privy Council Office for months and months. Could we have some production and not words?

BasePK: 3310602

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise and address a few remarks to the bill. I will endeavour to make my remarks relevant. I am sure Your Honour will appreciate that in supporting the bill and in making reference to the increase asked for, some of my remarks and suggestions may tend to be a little irrelevant.
July 2, 1981

However, I want to explain to the House why we are supporting the bill.
The bill is divided into two main parts. The first deals with the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program and the second with public housing.
I listened with great interest to the remarks of the minister. He made reference to requests from all sides of the House for assistance to the public with respect to housing. I appreciate that the requests from his side of the House must be as numerous and worthwhile as those from this side, and I appreciate that the government is paying lip service, in any event, by raising ceilings to a commitment to public housing. However, I would like to say to the minister that the raising of a ceiling does not indicate commitment. What matters is what is done, within the limits this House approves-with the programs the government will bring forward in addition to the current very worth-while programs, to substantiate the spending of money. It is not exactly raising the ceiling but what is supporting the ceiling that hon. members on this side of the House are interested in.
I and others in this House have been very critical of the government with respect to the chaos in the housing sector today. In terms of housing starts, which are technically up but literally down, in April the pre-sales contractors across Canada had translated the housing starts into a boom-on paper-but we know they will flatten out in the latter months of the summer because builders are just not building "spec" houses any more. As a result, emphasis on residential rehabilitation is very important, and for that reason our party is pleased to support this bill.
We also have problems, which the Liberal interest rate policy is causing throughout the country, with respect to mortgage interest rates. The rate is now at a record Liberal high of 18.5 per cent. People are just not buying new homes any more. They are forced to stay where they are, and the maintenance of rental housing is becoming all important to Canada. I point out that we are talking about rehabilitating housing and about vacancy rates; this government has created a real crisis with respect to apartment vacancy rates.
In April, 1979 the vacancy rate in Canada was 3.6 per cent. The acceptable average across Canada is 3 per cent. In April, 1981, by dint of indifference and by a real and determined effort at nothing at all, this government has brought the vacancy rate down to 1.8 per cent. In areas such as metro Toronto, which the minister represents, it is 0.4 per cent. People across Canada are having a difficult time finding places to live. It is no longer a question of adequate and decent shelter; it is a question of finding a place to live. For that reason we are certainly prepared to support this program.
We know that older housing requires extensive renovation. We have reviewed the very excellent report prepared for the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation entitled "An evaluation of RRAP," which is the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program. I have looked with interest at some of the recommendations in the report. I note, for example, that the eligibility under RRAP has changed. It is interesting to me as
National Housing Act
the spokesman for housing on this side of the House that the number one recommendation on page 121 has been adopted by the government, and I commend the government for that. It is also interesting to note that the income limit for family homes has been increased from $6,000 to $9,000. It is very unfortunate that AHOP owners who were led down the garden path in 1976 have found that this very same government-there has been a 50 per cent increase-has decided, instead of using 25 per cent of family income as the upper limit for AHOP eligibility, to raise that limit to 30 per cent. On behalf of the thousands of Canadian home owners who are renewing their mortgages under AHOP I suggest to the government that it would do very well to go back to the standard of 25 per cent on the basis of which these people were inveigled into buying homes and to go back to its original principles and take a hard look at the funding which is provided within this ceiling.
The minister referred to co-operation between federal and provincial levels. We do not want to see the same thing happen to this program that happened to the community services contribution program, under which muncipalities across Canada entered into three-phase programs with the understanding that the Government of Canada would stand behind its commitment to the cities, towns and villages of Canada to provide services. The government pulled out of the program and left municipalities across Canada high and dry looking for funding for two and three-phase programs in which they had become involved at the exhortation of the government. Many municipalities involved in this program have gone to a considerable amount of effort to set up their procedures, and I suggest that the government consider seriously the termination of these programs, if they are terminated, on a very orderly basis.
As far as the public housing part of the bill is concerned, we are supportive of anything this government does to help Canadians find decent, affordable housing in sound community environments. We on this side know that the shelter allowance has been the favourite trial balloon of this government. Shelter allowances have been created and hiked prior to national housing conferences only to have the balloon deflated two weeks later when the conferences were over and all the delegates had gone home. I hope this government under this increased ceiling will take a hard look at shelter al [...truncated]

BasePK: 3310654

Speech:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of great concern to many Canadians. Considering that the purpose of government policies and agencies is theoretically to assist and not impair Canadians in pursuit of legitimate goals; considering that many small business enterprises, already imperilled by this government's high interest rate policy, are further threatened by the unhappy situation in the government-operated Post Office; and considering that many small business enterprises such as Beaven's Custom Cannery in Summerland, British Columbia, are seasonal enterprises and that any disruption in normal mail communication with customers at this time threatens the entire annual production and profitability, without which the business must fail; I move, seconded by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling):
That immediate steps be taken to get the mails moving again, if necessary through back to work legislation.

BasePK: 3310688

Speech:
Madam Speaker, as I indicated, the reserves are at an historically low level, certainly over the last ten years. In relation to our trade they are at a very, very low percentage of our total activity.
Let me put my second question touching on this matter to the Minister of Finance. Bill Jarvis, an economist with Infor-metrica, stated that investor uncertainty over Canadian policies, especially in energy, is continuing to put our dollar under pressure and that a solution to the energy dispute between Ottawa and Alberta would go a long way toward strengthening the dollar and the reserves. If the government could settle the energy question, is it not true that it would relieve the outgo of Canadian dollars considerably, an outgo on petroleum

July 3, 1981
Oral Questions
products alone which was up 36 per cent in May of this year compared with May, 1980, due largely to the almost ludicrous position taken by the federal government of being willing to buy from a foreigner but not from our provinces such as British Columbia or Alberta?
Hon Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance): Madam Speaker, I do not want to be contentious with the hon. member about foreign exchange reserves, but I would suggest that when he compares the reserves of ten years ago he might look at the comparative prices for gold and translate into current market value the reserves of gold which we hold at the present time. But that is by way of suggesting that the hon. member reconsider his point.
With respect to the energy settlement, it is as clear to me, as it is to others, that there would be a number of benefits flowing from an energy settlement including, we would hope, the end of production cutbacks which are putting additional strain on our balance of payments. That in itself would improve the situation.
Furthermore, an energy settlement would remove an uncertainty which presently exists, and that would be helpful. It is for these reasons that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and his counterpart in Alberta have been working very constructively in their last meetings in order to reach an energy settlement.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I was thinking about finishing the speech I started earlier today, but in view of the fact that I have another important issue to raise, I will not do that but, rather, I will continue at another time to speak on Bill C-53.
What I wish to talk about tonight is the peculiar attitude- and one can only describe it as peculiar-taken by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) with respect to the question of the postal strike. Any thinking Canadian or legislator in this chamber must have deep concern about the consequences and effects of a postal strike on the average citizen. I am not talking about big business or medium-sized business, but about the average, so-called well-defined little guy who lives in each and every one of our constituencies. I am talking about the pensioner, the person who does not necessarily receive a government cheque, but many of whom rely on the mails for whatever little income they receive from some trust company or some small investment. I am talking about the little businessman. In an area such as mine, in Saskatoon, which is not a large city, and in the surrounding district I represent, substantial inconvenience is caused to those people who rely on the mails by virtue of a postal strike. I raised this matter in the course of question period yesterday. I tried to bring to the Prime Minister's attention some of the serious consequences which will flow as a result of this strike. I called on the government and the Prime Minister to take some action to deal with this strike before the House adjourns, which has been anticipated to be this coming Friday.
Regular mail delivery is an essential service for millions of individual Canadians, particularly for those in remote areas, for the pensioners and small businessmen I referred to. Pensioners who do not live in major urban centres are faced with the prospect of either a long period without income or a long
and difficult trek to a distant town. I suggest that Canada's senior citizens should not be forced to be pawns in the government's game of chess with the Post Office. Those in remote areas lack the same access to couriers as those in major urban centres. They rely heavily on the mails for communication with the rest of Canada.
I pointed out to the Prime Minister, as has been pointed out to him a number of times before, it is estimated that some
1,000	to 1,500 small businesses will go bankrupt for each week the strike continues. The cost to the Canadian economy will be between 6,000 and 9,000 jobs. The Canadian Direct Mailing Association estimates that its members will lose $2.9 million for each day the strike continues. This matter cannot be allowed to continue to drift without some government action. At the moment the two sides are not even talking, which 1 suggest is primarily due to the failure of the Treasury Board to bargain in good faith.
An interesting article appeared in the Toronto Star last weekend in which the labour reporter John Deverell suggested that on the basis of his information an examination of the attitude of the federal government with respect to the postal strike is one which is a kind of scenario situation. The only similar situation I can liken this to is with respect to the infamous cabinet document which dealt with the constitutional strategy which we all remember so vividly. In the case of the postal strike there was a scenario set down as to how the minister and the government could be perceived as being tough, holding the line and curtailing inflation. In other words, the kind of government cynicism toward the consequences which the postal strike will have on the Canadian people, in effect, turns out to be the second prong of its anti-inflation program. I remind the House that the first prong is the high interest rate factor. The second prong is a sort of facade which it is now putting on to be tough on a high profile union which does not have any popularity in Canada. In fact, it is one of the least popular unions in Canada.
However, this is a kind of facade which I suggest the government is putting up. It says, on one hand, "We will not go back to bargaining. We will not take any initiatives with respect to negotiations. We will sit back and let Canadians suffer through a long strike."
On the other hand, it says it will not take any legislative action. It is not going to negotiate. I suggest it is an obligation for the government to legislate. Either the government must return to the bargaining table to bargain in good faith, or it must take action to legislate an end to this strike. I would be most interested in hearing the views of the government as to why-and it cannot be serious-it is going to have this House adjourn without taking some steps with respect to the resolution of this matter. We cannot have Parliament adjourned, the only instrument which can allow the matter to be brought to resolution, until the middle of October, which is the proposed time for the adjournment according to the government House leader. We have a responsibility as legislators here.
July 7, 1981

I will be interested in hearing whether the response of the government is really and truly serious about its determination to cause the people of Canada the suffering that it intends to cause them by sitting back, doing nothing and taking no action either by negotiation or legislation.

These lawyers were not changed; they are the ones chosen way back by Mr. Bertrand himself. They know more about the case, 1 suspect, than anyone on this or that side of the House. Your findings led him to ask the Minister of Justice to prosecute." The Minister of Justice turned around and said, "Please, you do the prosecutions. You know the facts. We do not want to be suspected of hiding anything. You prosecute those very people that you said might be guilty."

Mediation in a difficult dispute when the parties have strongly entrenched positions is not something that is usually or ordinarily achieved in a day or two. There are members who are here who are familiar with industrial relations, and who are fully aware that the task of a mediator is a very delicate one. Sometimes it may take a week, sometimes two weeks, sometimes even longer than that to reach a settlement.
One of the great mediators and conciliators of the past few years is Senator Carl Goldenberg. He participated in many important disputes and was able to resolve a good percentage of them. I want to put on the record what Senator Goldenberg once said. It is applicable to the situation with which the Leader of the Opposition has confronted us today. He said that you cannot mediate in a goldfish bowl. No one can mediate if the parties have someone, an organization or a group, such as this, peering over one's shoulder every day.
The hon. member for Ontario seemed to admit this when he said that they had held back today from asking any questions on the subject of the strike so that Judge Alan Gold could start his mediation tomorrow. Let me discuss the dispute and the system we have for settling disputes between parties in the public service. The question arises whether people in the public service should have the right to strike. Often you hear the basic question as to whether people should have the right to strike at all. Summer Recess

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Bill C-252 is to provide an element of predictability in the calling of federal general elections at fixed dates, thereby replacing British North America Act section 50 which reads as follows:
Every House of Commons shall continue for five years from the day of the return of the writs-
Section 50 could be repealed or amended to read as follows:
Every Parliament shall continue until dissolved by the Governor General, which shall be not sooner than four years less forty days, nor later than four years plus forty days-
In fact , it would be established that general elections would be called at fixed dates every four years.
Of course, when the bill was introduced in the House, one of its supporters, the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone), emphasized certain positive aspects, but with very little conviction, it must be admitted. It has been said, for instance, that if the dates were fixed we would be able to gather on Parliament Hill on July 1 and hand out certificates and other things. That is a positive aspect of rather limited value. On the other hand, we must recognize that such a decision, in my opinion, would lead to radical changes in the operation of Canada's current political system. A government in office must indeed enjoy a certain flexibility. It will always be argued that such a flexibility will be used only for political and partisan purposes, the fact of being able to extend a mandate somewhat, and hon. members opposite believe that the intent is simply to leave enough room for the government to call the elections at the best time, at the most appropriate opportunity.
However, it must also be realized that in order to administer the country properly and run the country's business, a government must have a certain flexibility. It must be realized as well that at times when crises occur and a government cannot set a date to adjourn Parliament and simply forget what is happening. For all these reasons, I find it somewhat strange to have such a bill before the House when we have so many more important matters to discuss. We could discuss setting fixed dates for sessions, such as is the case for the National Assembly in Quebec. We would then know when the session would begin and when it would end. There are many other
important issues that could be discussed in this House. We could talk about parliamentary reform.
However, I do not believe that the bill now before the House should receive so much attention or deserves as much consideration as the hon. member opposite seems to want to give it. 1 shall therefore be very brief and simply say, Mr. Speaker, that I do not consider it most urgent or necessary to approve this bill. In my opinion, if we were to decide that this bill is more important than we realize, I would prefer that it be referred to a subcommittee to be studied in depth. However, for my part, Mr. Speaker, I do not agree that this is so, and I must say that I really cannot support this bill.

When I look at a piece of legislation, I always ask myself the following questions: who will win, who will lose, who will benefit and who will not benefit. Immediately I see that the person who will not benefit is the prime minister of Canada. He would lose the power to call a general election at his convenience.

John Diefenbaker, who suffered the most significant loss of parliamentary seats that has ever been suffered by a prime minister. Such was the majority gained in 1958 that he was able to continue in power until 1963. In 1963 the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker lost the confidence of the House of Commons and he was eventually defeated at the polls. In 1965, the Right Hon. Lester Pearson called an election without a cause. He was rebuffed by the electorate. In 1968 an election was called by the newly elected leader of the Liberal Party who later became prime minister, the Right Hon. Pierre Trudeau. He received a substantial majority in that election. In 1972 he called an election at his convenience and was severely rebuffed by the electorate. He hung on to power with two seats. In 1974 the House of Commons again voted non-confidence in the Trudeau government, but his government was restored to power by the people of Canada.

time, our people will blame the national government. They will not look to the provincial governments. I say in all sincerity to all members of the House that we should be wary of this. Early man lived in peace with his environment by fishing and hunting and foraging for food. For thousands of years, mankind on earth saw literally no environmental damage. He lived only by his own energy and that of his helpers in the group. The dawn of agriculture, in the history of mankind, was what Alvin Toffler, in The Third Wave, called the First Wave. In this era, one saw mankind live still in comparative harmony with nature. Energy sources, in addition to manual, were water, horses and oxen, forests, some coal for heating, and wind in some areas. Energy sources were such that the environmental damage was minimal.
Some considerable destruction took place over wide areas of the old world during the agricultural era. While the era extended over a period of several thousands of years, varying by area, it was only a glimpse when compared with the length of the previous era of which I spoke. For the first time, the agricultural era saw man experience the feeling that he had to conquer nature, that mankind was against nature. This idea was born in the agricultural era. Certainly mankind found itself in an uphill battle with nature and his environment.
The next era, which we call the industrial revolution, or the Second Wave, as Toffler referred to it, lasted less than 500 years; some would say 300 or just slightly over. The era was ushered in by the steam engine, and the history of this period, the industrial revolution, is well known to every one of us. We know that for energy during this period man turned to the steam engine, to electricity from water and later from coal, and hydrocarbons and uranium. Later during this period the internal combustion engine was the big user of hydrocarbons.
During the latter part of the industrial revolution, we had the use of nuclear fission. These energy sources, particularly hydrocarbons and nuclear fission, put our land, our water and our air at risk. The long-term effects of carbon dioxide on the atmosphere gives many people grave concern. The supply of hydrocarbons is diminishing. However, it is very important to note that many think the use of hydrocarbons will come to an end, not because of supply but because of the damage to our environment. That is why the recommendations with respect to this matter are found in this report to which I earlier referred.

However, we also see it from my former province of Nova Scotia, by the way, in tidal power. We see the use of wind in the future, photovoltaics, the continuation of nuclear fission. We see fuel cells, and in the long term we see nuclear fusion. 1 will have something to say about that later.

It was a year ago approximately to the day that the National Energy Program was introduced in Parliament, in October, 1980, and Bill C-48 came into being. At that time the opposition vehemently criticized the government for delaying the implementation of such important and much needed legislation.
I am somewhat amused to hear the comments of the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson). Last December 11 with reference to this bill he said:

The hon. member is pressing us to take action.
What has happened since then? In January, the bill was referred to the House of Commons Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works. Committee members deliberated for some 135 hours. The hon. member for Etobicoke Centre is quite right when he pays tribute to all of those people who participated right through from January to June of this past year. There were 140 witnesses and related experts who appeared before the committee. Well over 100 amendments from all three parties were considered during these hearings which resulted in 3,200 pages of testimony and, as a result, a number of amendments have taken place.
In July 1981 the committee reported back to this House on the bill. Speech:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday, at the end of the day, I was half way through my speech on what were then seven environmental motions which would amend Bill C-48 at the report stage of Parliament's deliberation on the legislation. With Your Honour's indulgence, with the remaining time, I now wish to complete my remarks. All of those motions relate to Clause 80 of Bill C-48, concerning oil-spill type pollution from resource activities on Crown lands and standards for compensation to parties hurt by it. Motion No. 4, as I understand it, would actually amend Clause 2, not Clause 80, by adding a definition of "spill". The proposed definition would, I think, helpfully broaden what is considered a violation of the environment under the legislation.
Motion No. 51 would remove any distinction between an authorized and an unauthorized spill for the purpose of, for example, awarding damages to an offended party. To my mind, Motion No. 51 makes a lot of sense on the grounds that pollution is pollution whether the source is authorized or not. Moreover, damage to either the general environment or to a party's property is no less severe just because the cause is authorized.
My party and I welcome Motion No. 52, which would require that the proper authority be informed beforehand of any authorized pollution, and that the same authority, in turn, give immediate notice to the aboriginal peoples and others who may be harmed by the discharge. Perhaps such requirements will, for example, help the native peoples protect themselves against pollution from activities at their back door. At the very least, if I may say, these people will know what is being done to their habitat in the face of resource development in their area.
Motion No. 53 substantially clarifies the liability of anyone who has violated the environment under the terms of the bill. It does so by specifying that compensation must be paid when pollution impairs, for example, one's source of income through loss not only of personal property but also of the natural environment from which the income is produced. To my mind, this motion would make the bill much more sensitive to the particular circumstances of native peoples, who are often hurt more by the indirect effects of pollution than by its direct impact on their personal property. In my view, in the view of my party and I think in the view of others in the House, compensation should be paid in either instance.
I must confess that the import of the minor amendment-I think it is minor-proposed by the Minister of Energy in Motion No. 55 escapes me, so I shall reserve judgment until a fuller explanation is provided, perhaps by the parliamentary secretary who was in the House a few moments ago and who no doubt will be speaking later.
October 15, 1981

Certainly Motion No. 56 has my full support, for it rightly seeks to recognize in the bill itself that damage to the environment often becomes discernible long after the actual offence has been committed. Thus, any time limit on when a claim for compensation may be instituted must be sensitive to such situations. At present, Bill C-48 does not reflect that reality. I welcome Motion No. 56 because it attempts to redress the problem.
Motion No. 57 would require the minister to launch a public inquiry into any activity that violates the environment by the standards of the bill. As the legislation stands, the minister may initiate an inquiry, and I stress the words "may initiate". But he is not required to do so. In my view, the minister should be required to do so under specified conditions.
We have dealt with Motion No. 54 and I have expressed myself on that question. I regret that it was not included in the original grouping of the motions under debate now. Let me stress that the Canadian Arctic Resources Committee was very much in favour of the idea behind Motion No. 54. I think the motion as expressed and moved reflects pretty well the import of the representation made vigorously by CARC and it certainly reflects something of my own thinking on the question.
If I may conclude, the bill before us at the report stage will govern the way in which some $300 billion will be spent on the exploitation of energy resources on Crown lands in the next decade alone. Some $300 billion will be spent in the next ten years, but trillions of dollars will be spent by the end of the century. It is clear that the government intends to have only a tiny proportion of such large amounts devoted to the protection of the environment. That will be of as much concern to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) as it is to me.
Worse still is the government's decision to perpetuate in Bill C-48 its habit of entrusting environmental responsibilities, not to the Minister of the Environment, who I see in the House today, but rather to ministers whose principal preoccupation and mandate are the promotion of resource activities that pose the greatest threat to the environment. The resultant conflict of interest is so apparent that one is hard pressed not to assume it constitutes a deliberate effort on the part of the government to undermine the role and responsibilities of the Minister of the Environment himself.
If we do anything else today and in subsequent days in the context of these motions, it should be to redress that very serious problem which I think is more fundamental than the specific problems addressed in the motions themselves being discussed this afternoon.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak in this debate, although I have only five minutes to speak on such a detailed matter that would require half an hour. I believe that if all government agencies and Crown corporations were to pay grants equal to the amount of taxes paid by private agencies in the various areas of Canada, it would mean these agencies and corporations not only would still have to pay the full amount of grants for their lands and buildings as they now have to, but also grants in lieu of business occupancy taxes. The previous speaker dealt with the business occupancy tax, and indicated the very valid reasons why that tax should not apply. I now intend to show why it is appropriate to exclude from their grant programs building units owned by them, in the same way those units are excluded from departmental grants applicable to property holdings.
The only class of facilities which might be included without giving rise to considerable pressure for the inclusion of other
classes in the grant program would be machinery and equipment. However, the arguments raised against grants for facilities are equally valid for machinery and equipment, including the very erratic way in which the latter are taxed or not taxed in the various areas of Canada when they are owned by the business community of the private sector.
Now, machinery raises administrative problems due to the fact that certain types of equipment are part of buildings. According to the general principle applied, even if a piece of machinery may be within a building and fixed to it, it is not considered to be part of that building, except if it is used in some way in its operation like, for instance, elevators, escalators, boilers, plumbing systems, air conditioning units, sprinklers, etc., which are all considered to be part of the building and are liable for grants in the case of buildings owned by Crown corporations or government departments.
Notwithstanding the different ways in which these matters are dealt with by individual provinces, the various types of buildings are not all taxed when they belong to the private sector. In this context and in view of the difficulties which might stem from the payment of grants on some buildings in some provinces and the non-payment of grants on similar facilities in other provinces, something which might jeopardize the universal nature of the grants program, it was felt that all Crown constructions had to be excluded.
This firm position concerning facilities is based on several other reasons. First of all, if one type of property were included in the grant scheme, there would be strong pressures, for other types to be subjected to the scheme, for it does not seem logical to include some while excluding others. Also, if all facilities were to give rise to grants, Crown corporations would have to agree, for this is provided for under Section 8(1 )(f) of the 1980 legislation. This decision would prove very costly to a number of Crown corporations to the point where they could no longer meet their obligations.
On the other hand, and this has nothing to do strictly speaking with facilities, few people are aware that under the grants program administered by the federal government, grants are paid in respect of some classes of buildings which would not be taxed were they to belong to other organizations. I should mention, by way of conclusion, schools, hospitals, penitentiaries, fire halls, etc.

In fact, a conventional diesel powered railway train operating with a high load factor will consume only about 700 energy units, referred to in the old jargon as British thermal units per seat mile, and an electric train will consume only about 150 energy units per seat mile, as compared with 2,000 to 7,500 energy units per seat mile for conventional automobiles, depending on the number of passengers, and 2,700 to 5,000 Btu's per seat mile for passenger aircraft. Mr. Speaker, let me begin by dealing with the matter that is before us, unlike some other speakers in this debate we have just heard tonight. Let me just outline for the record that the matter before us is a matter of motions that basically amend Clause 10 of Bill C-48. That clause in turn deals with the matter of exploration agreements and the ministerial discretion involved in the issuance of these exploration agreements. I merely wanted to put that on the record to show that very little in legislation is ever new. Any person who has experience in legislative matters or has involved himself in legislation in the provinces of Canada or in the federal Parliament will know these are simply regurgitated provisions from other statutes. Anybody who has dealt with urban planning will recognize these provisions as what is known in that field as "contract planning".
What these provisions do is very simply this: after enacting very complicated statutory provisions with great restrictions and protections, the provisions allow you to simply set them aside, sit down with a person who may be a friend, or a person with whom you can deal at arm's length, and write whatever deal you want to write. That is what an exploration agreement can do. That is why we are concerned with this matter and that is why we want some amendments to make sure that any exploration agreement which is written will be fair and will have the protection of other provisions of the act which check ministerial discretion. That is why we are here tonight.
I could go on and talk about the specifics of the bill, but I am afraid earlier speakers have got me off that subject. I want to deal with the remarks by the parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Etobicoke North (Mr. MacLaren), because I never heard such a massive distortion of the National Energy Program and the effect it is having and is going to have on Canada and Canadians.
I will dismiss my friend from the NDP to my left by simply saying this. It would be nice to think that all Canadians were willing to sit down and pool all the resources in one pot and divide them up by the number of people in Canada. That is not the way the system works, and it never will work that way. Those people had better start to realize that and they had better start dealing with the practicalities and realities of Canadian life.

For example, we would try to protect small Canadian business by having Petro-Canada supply independents with gasoline. There would not be any price gouging. native corporations I expect to be set up when land claims are settled. This is in fact a different way of approaching the issue.

The stakes in the energy play are simply enormous. I quote from an article in today's Globe and Mail by R. Donald Pollock. Mr. Pollock is chairman of the industrial policies committee of the Science Council of Canada. He says that in 1980-and he is talking about these stakes-

The figure is expected to go above 40 per cent by 1990. Unless Canada can reduce the level of foreign ownership in this sector, foreign firms will have the cash-flow from Canada's petroleum resources to acquire even larger sections of the Canadian economy or to ship out profits on a massive scale.
There it is put rather succinctly. If we do not have that control in Canada, we will see ourselves open to a capital strike, which we have seen. When my friends on the right get up and talk about rigs going south, that is a capital strike. All the lobbyists and pressure on the government, the price pressure on oil, results basically from foreign companies taking capital out of Canada. Again, I think we have the impression from the rhetoric surrounding Bill C-48 and from reading the various clauses that, in fact, Canadian control and ownership will be occurring in Canada's frontier lands and offshore developments. However, it works this way: Imperial is 70 per cent foreign owned. Therefore, 70 per cent of 70 shares equals 49 shares foreign owned. Thirty per cent Canadian owned of Imperial's 70 shares equals 21 shares. Petro-Canada, which is in the project for 30 per cent, is 100 per cent Canadian-owned, as we all know; therefore, its 30 shares are Canadian owned. Therefore, Imperial's 21 shares plus Petro-Canada's 30 means a 51 per cent'Canadian-owned project. However, the original partnership still gives Imperial not 51 per cent control but 70 per cent control. Certainly control is where the action is as opposed to the simple ownership.

We in the New Democratic Party want majority control as well as majority ownership. When we look at countries in situations similar to Canada, virtually every country we can examine has developed a strong policy which would equal Canadianizing as we know it in this country. But certainly the incentive is not there either; for when one looks at the American petroleum industry, which companies obviously own and control that industry? American companies own and control it. What I am saying is that we will not get any oil out of the frontier areas before 1990. We are not going to have very much in the way of new conventional production and the oil sands will not be in production. What is the alternative? We are going to be importing a million barrels of oil a day in 1990. That is how I see it. Are we going to put ourselves in the hands of OPEC, the Arab sheiks, and in the hands of other OPEC countries who may not be quite so friendly? Is that where we want to take our country? Do we want to make our country dependent upon OPEC when we have the reserves to do the job?
This legislation before us in Bill C-48 is not legislation that will encourage production in our frontier areas. The National Energy Program certainly is not going to encourage production from the oil sands or from conventional producing areas. What this legislation before us this afternoon, Bill C-48, does and what the whole National Energy Program does is what I referred to when I said we were playing Russian roulette with the life and economic future of our country. Members opposite do not understand that, and that is why I say I do not think they know what they are doing. Wake up before it is too late.
I had quite a number of other comments to make, Mr. Speaker, but I would like to finish with this. Let us put aside the question of foreign investment in the Canadian oil industry and let us put aside economic nationalism for the moment. Do we want to be known by our friends abroad as a government that steals? Do we want to be known as cheats and thieves? This legislation will put Canada at the top of the list of thieves and robbers. The government is taking property away retroactively. It is confiscating that property with virtually no compensation.

Order Paper Questions

BasePK: 3322863

Speech:
I would like to thank the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) for precipitating this discussion by bringing in this private member's bill. I know it is an issue that he is very familiar with and that he has spent many years working toward trying to improve the operation of the House with regard to matters of this nature. When we look at this issue, Mr. Speaker, I think it is necessary to look at how the Commissioners of Internal Economy came to have the jurisdiction that they have and where they came from.
The Commissioner of Internal Economy was established at the first session of Parliament. At that point, Mr. Speaker, Parliament met only a few weeks each year. Most of the employees employed by Parliament in those earlier days were mostly clerks and messengers who were employed on a temporary basis. They were employed for a few weeks or a couple of months at the most. Patronage was not unknown in those days; in fact, it was common and rather rampant. In 1867 and shortly thereafter it was desirable-and, as we all know that practice has long since died out and has become more or less extinct, at least at the federal level-that members from outside the Ottawa area, from more distant parts of Canada, should have jurisdiction over who was employed by Parliament on a temporary basis and who received these jobs. It was felt that to put this in the hands of members from the Ottawa area would be giving Jack the Ripper an Avon route. Perhaps it would result in some great injustices.
To protect Parliament in those days, the Board of Commissioners of Internal Economy was set up. The only members from outside the Ottawa area who were here all year round were cabinet ministers. In conducting research into the historical development of the existence of the Board of Commissioners of Internal Economy, I found that that seems to have been the rationale for the reason why they wound up doing the job they have been doing for so many years.
A few years ago, the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization, recognizing the immensely more complex administrative requirements of the House in the late twentieth century, recommended the creation of the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services so that members, other than the Speaker and ministers, could participate in the administrative decisions of the House. I think it is fair to say that probably most of the best improvements in the administration of the House have originated from this committee.
I think it could be argued that the situation does need review. This committee often meets in camera and rarely reports to the House. This does not mean to say that the members on the committee are unaware of its deliberations or its advice.
Furthermore, it is important to bear in mind that the committee does not have any executive authority in law. It remains with the Commissioners of Internal Economy. The committee can review the situation and hold what discussions they feel are appropriate and make whatever recommendations they feel are appropriate. In the final analysis, they do not have legal authority. This is something that has rested with the Commissioners of Internal Economy and continues to rest with them.
An example that we might look at is the Senate. These days some people tend to view the Senate as a bit of an anachronism in many ways. I suppose that is an issue that can be argued. Perhaps the example of the Senate is worth looking into. When you look at the Senate, you will find that almost all the administrative decisions that are taken there are not taken by the Speaker or in camera or by a body that does not report to the whole House, but by a standing committee that is accountable to the Senate.
What is the result of this? In recent months there have been many rumours and allegations, some of them perhaps based on fact, others on fiction. There have been counterclaims about the administration and the machinations that go on in the House. Of course, we have the nation's gossip columnists. Many of the political columnists have had a heyday talking about the debates and internal dissension that have, in fact, occurred.

That company was the Dart Container Line. Their departure from the port of Halifax became a matter of major and serious concern. Subsequently and more recently, in September 1981, another major user of the port of Halifax, Trans-Freight Line indicated it would discontinue its service to the port of Halifax. While it has a Canadian connection, it is basically a foreign-owned company.
Adjournment Debate

There are rules regulating the contents of the householder mailings, but members must take full responsibility for material mailed under their frank and written on official stationery.

-a political, partisan or party nature-

(iv) election campaign material-
I would suggest this would fall into that class. It includes:
(v) publications normally made available by party headquarters.

Because they printed this one, they obviously felt it did not contravene the guidelines. Since we have removed that responsibility from the bureaucrats, I will not give it back to them. I will look at this householder against the guidelines set by the committee to see whether they need to be further clarified.
Members should keep in mind that what is partisan to one member is sometimes not partisan to another. From March 1, 1981, to March 1, 1983, the federal government will receive-I want hon. members to note this figure-$27.5 billion more on a national accounts basis. Who else benefits? The rich who are on salary benefit. This budget proposes cuts in marginal tax rates for people with high incomes. The whole great ends of this confederation may not be realized in the lifetime of many who now hear me. We imagine not that such a structure can be built in a month or in a year. Today we have the opportunity to complete and expand that structure. The resolution before this House provides for the patriation of the Constitution. After 114 years, Canada will finally have achieved its full legal independence. No longer will it be necessary to go to the Parliament of another country to amend our Constitution.

The resolution provides as well for an amending formula, that is, a mechanism which will enable us to make future changes to our Constitution. The first of these contributions I want to mention-because I think it is very important, given the regional nature of Canada-was that as a result of early discussions, broad new powers were given to the provincial governments over the development, control and management of their resources.

The amending formula was changed. The absolute veto for the Senate was dropped, and the Charter of Rights and Freedoms was modified to make it blend with our parliamentary tradition.

The answer is very simple, Madam Speaker. First of all, to everyone's surprise, the nine English-speaking provinces agreed to protect the education rights of francophones outside Quebec, which is a tremendous achievement and one which has given me great cause for rejoicing. There is still the matter of the courts and the proceedings in the legislatures. The Constitution of 1867 already provides for the use of both languages in the courts and legislatures in two cases, and this year we have made some progress because the government of New Brunswick has committed itself even further under Section 133, which provides francophones with better guarantees than those enjoyed by anglophones in Quebec. I do agree that it is unfortunate that Ontario has not decided to make French one of the languages used in the courts and in the Ontario legislature. However, in our charter and in our constitutional resolution, we have provided for a mechanism that will enable the provinces to make such changes through bilateral agreements, and I would ask the provinces to consider such action as soon as possible. In any case, we have made considerable progress by entrenching in the Constitution, here and now, that the Parliament of Canada and federal institutions shall always be bilingual.

November 24, 1981

So, in most of North America title was acquired from the Indian people by way of treaties or, in the United States where negotiations did not work or broke down, by war. The legal question of aboriginal property rights was not faced by the United States Supreme Court until 1955. The policy of treaties was established in Canada and enshrined by our forefathers in the Royal Proclamation of 1763.
By 1850, treaties had brought about the surrender of almost the whole of eastern Canada and were fast being made across the prairies. By 1885, Canada had its first major legal battle of aboriginal title, the now famous St. Catharines milling case. In that case the counsel for the province of Ontario argued: "We say that there is no Indian title at law or in equity. The claim of the Indians is simply moral and no more."
The St. Catharines milling case dealt with Treaty 3, the Lake of the Woods area in Ontario and, although related to aboriginal title, Indian people were never directly represented in the litigation. The real conflicting parties in the case were the interests sought by the governments of Canada and Ontario. Strangely enough, it was the logging company that argued that Canadian policy had always recognized Indian land rights. This affirmed, for the first time in Canadian law the legal, real property character of the Indian usufructuary title.
Judicial opinion has wandered somewhat since then. For example, in 1934 the Ontario Supreme Court said that the Crown could do whatever it wished, even with reserve land, whereas the exchequer court, as recently as in 1964, said in essence that Indian band land is the same as title in fee simple.
The great Metis leader, Louis Riel, twice elected to the Parliament of Canada, was hanged in 1885 for his views on aboriginal rights in western Canada.
By the turn of the century, politicians were fast moving to remove the rights of native people through abuses of human rights. In British Columbia, for example, my home province, in 1895 the right to vote was taken away from every Indian person in the province and was not returned until 1949. In the same year, 1895, the federal Department of Fisheries restricted the Indian food fishery. By 1915, Indian hunting and trapping was brought under strict provincial regulation, these actions at that time being taken against the population which was reduced from 50,000 in 1850 to 10,000 in 1900.
Ravaged by smallpox, forced on to small reserves and excluded from wage labour, it was illegal for Indian people in British Columbia to work and be paid for it. They were excluded from the fishery. They were excluded from their traditional hunting and guiding territories. They were excluded from forest activities and then they were put on reserves. It was not until 1960, in fact the 1963 federal election, less than 20 years ago, that native Canadians could first vote. We are just at the threshold of leaving the darkest of dark ages in the history of human rights violations by the Government of Canada done upon the indigenous people of this land. We have, therefore, allocated $4 billion to a Western Development Fund, of which we expect to spend $2 billion over the next three years... Specific development initiatives will be selected in consultation with the governments of the western provinces. They will be designed to address the major economic opportunities and constraints which will challenge the west during this decade. For example, the federal government is hopeful that through consultation with interested groups in the west, agreement can be reached on the modernization of the western grain handling and transportation system which is so vital to the growth and diversification of the prairie economy. We will also consider initiatives relating to industrial diversification and examine ways in which trade and industrial policies can better serve western development. To co-ordinate these efforts and to ensure early action, the Prime Minister has established a special group of ministers led by my colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
What has become of that plan? The government has forgotten about it. No consultations have been held and no plans have been drawn up for the spending of these alleged billions of dollars.
Indeed, one wonders whether the government really knew what it had created. The simple fact is that nobody in the government had any intention of putting in place seed money for the development of industry in western Canada. They simply needed a fund they could dip their hands into when the pot was empty somewhere else.
Adjournment Debate
In the budget, we can plainly see how completely fraudulent this fund really is and what a cruel hoax has been perpetrated on the people of western Canada by this government. The fund has now been slashed to $1.5 billion from $4 billion, to be spread over five years instead of three. This year's allocations are at $148 million, down $202 million from this year's main estimates. In the budget, the government announced that the allocations are all intended to provide for improvements in the western transportation system. Now we find that $65 million will be used to assist Vancouver in the purchase of urban transit, light rapid transit. All that equipment comes from eastern Canada. So much for providing jobs and secondary industry and technology to the west.
What is even more disturbing is the use of the fund to funnel $81 million to Canadian farmers for payment for losses sustained because of the Soviet grain embargo. Canadian farmers have every right to their money. They must be compensated fairly for their loss. This government, however, is paying money to them from a fund declared to be for the economic development of the west. One should add that of the $81 million payment, $13 million goes to farmers in Ontario and Quebec. Both payments should have been paid out of the general treasury.
Grain embargo moneys out of a fund purportedly designed to place seed money in western Canada for industrial and transportation improvement and expansion is a complete betrayal of promises to western Canada. The use of the fund to buy an eastern transit system for Vancouver means no new industry and jobs for western Canadians. When the pot gets dry, western Canadians will pay again as we have in the past. The fund, created to turn some resource profits back to western Canada to build the west, is a fraud simply and purely, a mirage, a joke.
With the envelope system of expenditures having been accepted by the government, any moneys dedicated to the Western Development Fund will be used as a slush fund by cabinet to loosen up moneys in the envelope for other parts of the country. Thus, perversely, the so-called Western Development Fund is actually the antithesis of that. The government's actions are another in a long series of broken promises to the west. It is no wonder that the Liberal Party is the laughing stock of western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it is 114 years since the Fathers of Confederation laid aside seemingly irreconcilable differences in the larger interests of the union of this country. The country itself was born, despite differences, and it grew in defiance of geography. Throughout the years, the plea for unity has become almost stale with frequent usage. The coin may be common, but it certainly is not debased.

November 25, 1981
The Constitution
When other countries laboured in blood and fratricidal strife for their very survival, Canadians struggled in controversy and frequently acrimonious debate.
However, if there was one outstanding quality which kept us together, surely it was the quality of faith, the faith of successive leaders that Canadians could prove to the world that a nation such as this, born in strife, diverse in its origins, speaking two languages and representing the embodiment of several great cultures, can survive and prosper. That faith has been tested on many occasions. There were those who questioned our will to survive as a nation. There were others who, recognizing the bone and the muscle of nationhood, queried whether or not we possessed the spirit of nationhood. The spirit of nationhood had to be embodied in a sense of patriotism which would put Canada ahead of its parts; and, for a fleeting period, that emotion was palpably evident in the year that marked Canada's centennial.
Finally, we had a distinctive, truly Canadian flag which became the symbol which helped erase the image and the idea of any kind of hyphenated Canadian. However, even the adoption of a distinctive flag was not sufficient to instil in all Canadians a sense of common purpose, a deep sense of pride in their country, and an abiding faith in its destiny. To a certain extent, Canada was a nation in search of an identity. After all, what did it really mean and what does it really mean to be a Canadian? Now, for the first time in 114 years, we are finally in a position to at least partially answer that question, an answer which probably would not have been supplied through the process of simple patriation.
Finally, we are able to establish in our own minds and in the minds of the rest of the world, the kind of people we really are, the vision of a country we intend Canada to be, and our deep commitment and loyalty to that country and to the principles by which we govern ourselves.
I have noticed, among some members of the public, and even of the media, a certain impatience that Parliament should devote so much time to constitutional matters when economic matters are so very pressing. My feeling is that unless we proclaim our determination to survive as a country, to live together, to work together and to build together a worth-while nation, we will be constantly assailed by economic forces to which the very lack of cohesion would leave us particularly vulnerable.
Finally, and in an awesome endeavour demanding a sense of responsibility which the importance of the question deserves, we are about to achieve that cohesion. However, even as I sense the euphoria of the moment, I am conscious-as, indeed, are all hon. members of the House-of the absence of one voice from the proclamation of common purpose. What is that purpose? It is to build a truly Canadian nation in which all its people will be known by their tolerance, fairness and determination to uphold the dignity and to acknowledge the intrinsic value of every man and every woman. It is on these very attributes of tolerance and fairness that I wish to dwell as I
believe they are the hallmark of the constitutional proposal now before us.
Perhaps I am in a unique position to be objective in analysing the Canadian identity for the simple reason that I am probably the newest Canadian in the entire House, inasmuch as citizenship was conferred on me only 11 years ago. Therefore, I am Canadian not by birth but very definitely by conviction. Unlike some people, I had a choice of countries to which I could have emigrated, and each of them probably could have offered me an equal amount of economic opportunity.
Why, then, did I specifically choose Canada? Fundamentally, it was because of my faith in Canada as an open, free, tolerant country which refused to remain prisoner of its own past but which was capable of reconciling the past with the present in one vibrant, throbbing hope for the future. I choose it too because of its immense size and the sense of grandeur, adventure and rich variety which that size denoted. In geography alone it offered me more wealth than any treasure trove of which I had ever read or dreamed. I believed that Canada would welcome me and my family, not despite our cultural background but, perhaps, even because of it. I believed that diversity was considered to be a challenge and even an asset rather than a pitiable or even contemptible liability. I believed that the only restrictions imposed on myself and on all members of my family were those of good common sense, our own ability and our own willingness to work.
My private faith in Canada and in the Canadian way of life has been fully justified. The daughter of a women who had to join the suffragette movement in order to obtain the right to vote is now, herself, a member of Parliament. The sister of a fully qualified veterinarian, denied a prominent government position because of his faith, can now proudly, and without fear of reprisal, claim from government benches, "I am a Catholic".
My personal odyssey through four countries has no doubt given me a perspective of freedom unseen by many who so blithely take freedom for granted. November 26, 1981

House to move a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.

Speech:
that Bill C-262, to amend the Canada Elections Act (publication of the result of opinion polls), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is certainly not the first time I have brought a bill before this House on this particular subject. As a matter of fact, it is at least the sixth time that this particular bill has been before Parliament in my name and has been debated. Prior to that, other hon. members in this House had felt the same way I feel about the publication of polls during election campaigns.
On one occasion, the government did take some specific action. My bill, and also one standing in the name of another hon. member were referred to the broadcasting committee, where we had a very long and useful discussion. At that time the committee came in with a recommendation that action be taken by the government which would eliminate the publication of opinion polls during actual election campaigns. The government did not move on that recommendation.

What I hope we might accomplish today, as far as this particular piece of legislation is concerned, is that it be referred to the appropriate standing committee of the House of Commons. The committee could then discuss the matter and come forth with a decision, expressing its views in relation to the matter of polls. If there were a supportive view from that committee regarding the banning of the publication of polls during election campaigns, appropriate legislation to put it into effect might then be forthcoming from the government.
At this moment, the only province in Canada which bans the publication of public opinion polls during election campaigns is the province of British Columbia. I have often used the example of the election of the Bennett government in British
Columbia which was predicted by no one because there were no polls to give guidance to the great fourth estate in coming up with conclusions.
However, that is only one example, and it is not the reason I believe public opinion polls should be banned from public discussion during election campaigns. What really gives me great concern is not the actual raw information which comes from polls, but the pollution resulting from experts on the media who speak only about numbers and never about issues during election campaigns. They put people into the position of playing numbers games, wondering who is ahead and who says who is ahead.
The greatest travesty of poll results which has ever been perpetrated upon the public was evident in the last election campaign in the United States. Pollsters in that country were on every network of radio and television, and reported in every newspaper one could imagine. They told the people of that country that the election between Ronald Reagan and President Jimmy Carter would be a cliff-hanger, too close to call, with less than 1 per cent dividing the opinions of the public. On election day, the end result was that the people in California did not have to bother going to the polls because the election was over before they even got there. For instance, the ABC network carried out a raw poll almost as soon as the TV debate was concluded. The poll stated more than just who the public felt was the winner of the debate; it stated that Ronald Reagan was the people's choice. However, even with all of this evidence, on November 3, the day before the election, the public was told that it was a toss-up, with Ronald Reagan one point ahead of Jimmy Carter. As it turned out, Ronald Reagan was not one point ahead of Jimmy Carter the next evening, he was nine points ahead. Even with all of the protectors the pollsters put into their predictions, they cannot, in justice, explain away the misdirection they gave to the United States public.
While I have never suggested the art of polling should be banned, nor that politicians and political parties should be deterred from using them at any time, I believe more strongly than ever that from the date an election campaign officially begins until it is finished, there should be no polling information made available to the public. What a change it would be for the electorate to make decisions based on leadership and programs rather than percentages!

Madam Speaker, as far as the legal aspect of the matter is concerned, obviously I can only express an opinion. The courts will have to decide on the legality aspect, if necessary, but my position has always been, that ever since I became leader of the Canadian government we have always looked for an amending formula based on the concept of regionalism, which recognized the existence of four regions in Canada and as a result acknowledged implicitly that the Province of Quebec had a veto right. That was our position at the constitutional conference in 1971, and has been our position up to the events of the past few weeks, when we had a resolution before the House in which we were proposing an amending formula based on the regional concept and therefore on a veto right for Quebec. So that when Premier Levesque, in joining forces with the seven provinces, agreed with their concept that all provinces were equal and that there were no veto rights for anyone, and signed the accord on April 16 of this year, he relinquished the veto right we had been prepared to acknowledge in the amending formula. So that is what happened, Madam Speaker, and once more, I do not want to say what the law is on this question nor what the constitutional conventions should be. I merely wish to say that for ten years we have been proposing a constitutional amending formula that would have given the Province of Quebec veto rights, and it was Mr. Levesque's government that since or sometime before the accord, in September 1980, joined forces with the seven provinces which denied veto rights to any of the provinces. Mr. Levesque agreed to accept this view, thereby relinquishing the veto rights we were prepared to acknowledge, not in law but in the amending formula we were proposing.

November 27, 1981

Mr. Speaker, on November 16, 1981, I directed a question to the Minister of State for finance (Mr. Bussieres) concerning the impact of the budget on the construction of rental units. The Minister of Finance for Mr. MacEachen if you recall, was out to lunch. Specifically, I pointed out that my investigations had shown that since the introduction of the budget, construction had ended on thousands of rental units from St. John's, Newfoundland to Vancouver.
I therefore asked the minister whether the government had anticipated that these projects would be halted, with thousands thrown out of work and millions of dollars worth of construction lost, when it brought down the budget.
I might add, Mr. Speaker, that in the next 24 hours after asking that question, it became apparent from my continued investigation, that the impact of the budget was even more staggering than was first apparent. Just five days after the introduction of the budget, my office was able to identify 13,000 rental units on which construction was halted or suspended. A conservative estimate indicated that this figure represented at least a billion dollars' worth of construction and over 10,000 jobs. The direct cause of this industry shut-down was one particular measure in the budget. The government disallowed the deductibility of soft costs of MURBs, making most of these projects instantly uneconomic. What is worse, this measure was, in effect, retroactive since it came into force on budget night. It thus affected all projects already under construction or very close to being started.
Since the lead time on these projects is usually more than a year, it thus seriously undermined the economic viability of projects that had been planned in good faith many months ago.
The minister's response to my question on November 16 was extremely unsatisfactory in light of the gravity of the situation that we face. He replied only that the government's fight against inflation would alleviate the problems of the housing sector since lower interest rates would stimulate demand for construction and the economy would thus benefit. I referred to this as the enema theory of fighting inflation-flushing out the economy.
Fortunately, the ridiculousness of this reply was apparent even to the Minister of Finance since, when I repeated my question to him the next day, giving him the new figures, he replied at once that he was willing to amend the budget and grandfather this particular measure.
Soft costs will now continue to be deductible on projects which have been started before December 31, 1981, as long as work on them proceeds without delay.
While we welcomed that announcement, I must point out to the minister that he has not diagnosed the problems. With his

For instance, the grandfather clause applies to projects started this year only. What about next year when construction on rental units will come to a halt? The minister has lowered the marginal tax rate, thus freeing more funds for high income Canadians, but he has done nothing to divert these funds into the creation of housing units. Under the MURB program, 20,000 to 30,000 units would have been built next year.
The government program of offering interest-free loans to builders is totally inadequate. The $7,500 loan limit is certainly not large enough to make investment by developers very attractive. In Vancouver it was suggested that this amount might pay for the construction of a bathroom. The limit of the program, 15,000 units, will not even solve the problems of Vancouver. Further, the program will not take effect for several months because consultation with the provinces is required. The government offers no help to renters who pay more than 30 per cent of their income on shelter.
What is the long-term problem that must be addressed, Mr. Speaker? Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation says that there is a shortfall in building nationwide, and that Canada needs 220,000 new housing units each year. Next year Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation estimates that starts will only amount to 135,000. That means a vacancy rate of zero by 1983 in most markets, according to CMHC. It means that rents will increase 20 per cent to 50 per cent in some markets and perhaps 100 per cent in Vancouver. It also means that a black market in rental units may develop. Families will have to start doubling up. We will witness a substantial regression in housing conditions following 35 years of gradual improvement. The problem is that the production of rental units is uneconomic. CMHC says that the average metropolitan rent across the country is $400 a month. The average investor carrying cost on a newly constructed unit with a 30 per cent down payment is $750 a month. This leaves a cash deficit of $350 a month before even allowing for operating costs. This is why incentives are necessary to attract funds into the construction of rental units.

There is already a waiting list of 20,000 people, with no place to go as there is no housing. I have to deal with these people who come to me, in true anxiety, wondering where they can find the money to pay these increases. The vacancy rate is 0.2 per cent, and it cannot go much lower.
